summary: This Wikipedia-derived note covers Pope Paul VI (Giovanni Battista Montini), focusing on his papacy and pastoral and ecumenical work. It describes his response to criticism of Humanae vitae, his creation of new Vatican offices for interreligious dialogue, non-believers and economic development, and his dialogue with Communist authorities. It also covers his role at Vatican II, his ecumenical outreach to Protestant churches, his Milan ministry, and the beatification process that followed a reported miracle.
one_line: Overview of Pope Paul VI's papacy, including Humanae vitae, Vatican II leadership, ecumenical dialogue, Vatican offices, and his beatification process.
key_facts: Paul VI reportedly told Edouard Gagnon on the eve of the encyclical, "in twenty years time they'll call me a prophet."

The Vatican biography states that "[t]he controversies over these two pronouncements tended to overshadow the last years of his pontificate," referring to priestly celibacy and contraception teaching.
Pope John Paul II later reaffirmed and expanded Humanae vitae with the encyclical Evangelium vitae.
In 1964, Paul VI created a Secretariat for non-Christians, later renamed the Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue.
In 1971, Paul VI created a papal office for economic development and catastrophic assistance and decreed an annual peace day on January first.
Paul VI received Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko and Nikolai Podgorny in the Vatican in 1966 and 1967 while seeking better conditions for Christians behind the Iron Curtain.
During his Milan period, Montini's 1957 campaign featured 7,000 sermons delivered by more than 500 priests in places including factories, hospitals and military barracks.
Paul VI opened the third session of Vatican II on 14 September 1964 and concluded it on 21 November 1964 with the formal pronouncement of Mary as Mother of the Church.
In December 2013, Vatican officials approved a supposed miracle attributed to Paul VI's intercession, the curing of an unborn child in California in the 1990s.
In February 2014, consulting Vatican theologians to the Congregation for the Causes of Saints recognized the miracle attributed to the late pontiff.
The Lutherans were the first Protestant Church to offer dialogue with the Catholic Church, in September 1964 in Reykjavík, Iceland.
The dialogue with the Methodist Church began in October 1965, and the Reformed Churches entered dialogue with the Catholic Church four years later.

Paul VI formally approved a joint Catholic-Protestant Bible translation on Pentecost 1967, after telling Cardinal Augustin Bea, "as far as the cooperation with Bible societies is concerned, I am totally in favour."
Montini reportedly said of John XXIII's announced council: "This old boy does not know what a hornets nest he is stirring up."
